in_text_mentions: The median age of onset for all patients was 20 days (7–23 days). The most common clinical symptoms were tachypnea, fever, and cough, occurring in 100%, 88.9%, and 77.8% of patients, respectively. Four patients exhibited moist rales on auscultation. Regarding clinical diagnosis, eight patients were diagnosed with pneumonia. Among these, four developed lung abscesses, and five exhibited extrapulmonary manifestations, including sepsis in two patients, skin abscesses in two patients, a liver abscess in one patient (Figure 1), and a brain abscess in one patient (Figure 2), among others.

in_text_mentions: ultiple patchy, large consolidations and mass opacities in both lungs in seven patients (87.5%), with some lesions appearing coalescent and ill-defined. Contrast-enhanced imaging revealed prominent non-enhancing hypodense necrotic changes within the lesions in three patients, clinically suggestive of lung abscess (Figure 4). Chest CT also revealed a cavitary lesion consistent with lung abscess in one patient. Of these four patients with lung abscess, Aspergillus fumigatus was identified in three, while Pa was detected in one. None of the patients exhibited hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Panel-specific HE histology of peritoneal biopsy showing organizing peritonitis with epithelioid macrophages/granulomatous features in a 2-year-old with genetically confirmed CYBB CGD presenting as aseptic ascites. Matches chronic granulomatous inflammation histology vocabulary. b: HE shows well-organized granuloma from peritoneal nodule biopsy that prompted CGD workup, confirmed by DHR and CYBB mutation. Direct granulomatous manifestation of CGD. c: CD163 IHC of same peritoneal granuloma showing non-expressing macrophages, part of CGD granuloma characterization in confirmed CGD case.Qualifies as granulomatous inflammation histology.
panels.attribution_text: Moreau et al. Chronic granulomatous disease presenting as aseptic ascites in a 2-year-old child.. Case reports in immunology 2013. doi:10.1155/2013/927897. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (a) Biopsy of peritoneal nodules demonstrated a cellular and organizing peritonitis including neutrophils, mesothelial cells, and abundant macrophages some with epithelioid features (HE, 200x). Focal areas had relatively well-organized granulomas (b) with macrophages that did not express the activated macrophage marker CD163 (c) ((b); HE, 200x, (c); CD163, 200x).
in_text_mentions: t for culture, and biopsies of the peritoneum were taken. The ascitic fluid had 1500 WBCs but was sterile. Pathology of the peritoneal biopsies revealed acute and organizing peritonitis with granulomatous features but no evidence of fungal, acid-fast, or bacterial microorganisms (Figure 1). The granulomatous nature of the peritonitis prompted evaluation for CGD. A dihydrorhodamine (DHR) test was performed to assess oxidase burst capability and resulted in negligible fluorescence, consistent with CGD. Genetic testing revealed hemizygosity for the c.1683dupG mutation in exon 13 of the CYBB gene.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Barium meal panel from X-linked CGD case 1 showing antral/pyloric luminal thinness and delayed emptying consistent with granulomatous gastritis with outlet obstruction. B: Same barium series as A, CGD case 1, showing gastric outlet narrowing. C: Barium meal panel from CGD case 1 showing delayed emptying and antral/pyloric thinness. D: Barium meal panel from CGD case 1 showing gastric outlet obstruction phenotype. E: Upper GI series from CGD case 2 showing antropyloric stenosis, direct match to granulomatous gastritis with outlet obstruction. F: Abdominal radiograph from CGD case 2 showing diffuse intestinal dilatation secondary to lower GI obstruction in context of antropyloric disease; mapped to GI obstructive granulomatous disease with proposed specific dilatation terms absent from vocabulary.
